cultural_context: Pizza shop setting familiar to students worldwide, real-world fraction applications in cooking and business
description: Welcome to your very own pizza shop! But here is the twist — every order, every recipe, and every slice involves fractions. Can you run a successful pizzeria while mastering halves, quarters, thirds, and more? Slice it right and your customers will keep coming back for more!

endings.message: You are the undisputed Master Pizza Chef! Your fraction skills are extraordinary — every slice is mathematically perfect, every recipe is precisely measured, and every customer gets exactly what they ordered. The food critic gave you 5 stars, the mayor declared 'Fraction Pizza Day' in your honor, and math teachers from all over bring their students to your shop. You proved that fractions are not just numbers — they are the secret ingredient to success!
endings.title: Master Pizza Chef

endings.message: Your Fraction Pizza Shop is the most popular spot in town! Customers line up every day because they know they will get exactly the right portions. Your reputation is solid, your team works like a well-oiled machine, and you have a real gift for making fractions fun. The shop is profitable and growing. You might not be a math genius yet, but you are well on your way!
endings.title: Popular Pizzeria

endings.message: Your pizza shop is doing okay — not great, not terrible. Some orders come out right, some are a little off. Customers are satisfied but not amazed. Your fraction skills improved but there is still room to grow. The foundation is there — with more practice, you could turn this into something special. Every expert was once a beginner!
endings.title: Average Joe's Pizza

endings.message: Your pizza shop is struggling. Too many orders went out with wrong fractions — customers who asked for 3/4 got 2/3, and complaints piled up. The good news? You learned from every mistake. Fractions are tricky, but every great chef had to practice before they got it right. Do not give up — come back and try again!
endings.title: Struggling Shop

endings.message: The pizza shop had to close its doors. Wrong fractions led to wrong orders, wrong orders led to unhappy customers, and unhappy customers stopped coming. But here is the thing — failure is the best teacher. Thomas Edison failed thousands of times before inventing the light bulb. Come back, practice your fractions, and try again. Your next attempt will be better!
endings.title: Closed for Business

glossary_terms.definition: A number that represents a part of a whole. Written as one number over another, like 3/4. The top number (numerator) tells how many parts you have, and the bottom number (denominator) tells how many equal parts the whole is divided into.
The top number in a fraction. It tells you how many parts you are talking about. In 3/4, the numerator is 3 — you have 3 parts.
The bottom number in a fraction. It tells you how many equal parts the whole is divided into. In 3/4, the denominator is 4 — the whole is split into 4 equal pieces.

Fractions that look different but represent the same amount. For example, 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8. You can create equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing both the numerator and denominator by the same number.
A shared denominator used when adding, subtracting, or comparing fractions. To add 1/3 + 1/4, convert both to twelfths: 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.
A number made up of a whole number and a fraction together, like 2 1/2 (two and a half). It means 2 whole things plus half of another one.
A fraction where the numerator is bigger than the denominator, like 5/2. It represents more than one whole. 5/2 is the same as 2 1/2.
Making a fraction as simple as possible by dividing the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor. For example, 4/8 simplifies to 1/2 (divide both by 4).

how_to_play: You run a pizza shop for 14 days — every order involves fractions!
Each round presents a kitchen challenge where you must use fractions to make decisions.
Watch your dashboard — your Kitchen Stations, Ingredients, and Customer Satisfaction are interconnected.
NPCs like Chef Maria (mentor), Delivery Dan, Picky Priya, and Marco react to your choices.
Random events like lunch rushes and food critic visits will test your fraction skills.
Keep your Math Accuracy high — wrong fractions mean unhappy customers and lost money!
learning_objectives: Understand and identify basic fractions (halves, thirds, quarters)
Add and subtract fractions with like and unlike denominators
Compare fractions to determine which is larger or smaller
Multiply fractions by whole numbers in real-world contexts
Recognize equivalent fractions in practical situations
Apply fraction concepts to solve real-world problems

choices.label: A. 3/8 — because 3 slices out of 8 equal slices is 3/8
choices.learning_concept: Understanding Fractions as Parts of a Whole
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A fraction represents parts of a whole. The denominator (bottom number) tells us the total number of equal parts — here the pizza is cut into 8 slices. The numerator (top number) tells us how many parts we're looking at — 3 slices. So 3 out of 8 equal slices = 3/8.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. 8/3 — because the pizza has 8 slices and we want 3
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You swapped the numerator and denominator. In a fraction, the top number (numerator) is the PART we want, and the bottom number (denominator) is the TOTAL number of equal parts. 3 slices out of 8 = 3/8, not 8/3.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. 3/5 — because 3 slices out of 5 remaining slices
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The denominator must be the TOTAL number of equal parts in the whole pizza (8), not the remaining slices (5). When we take 3 slices from a pizza cut into 8, the fraction is 3/8. The denominator always represents the whole.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. 1/3 — because we want one-third of the pizza
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 1/3 means 1 part out of 3 equal parts. But our pizza is cut into 8 equal slices, and we want 3 of them. The correct fraction is 3/8. Remember: denominator = total equal parts, numerator = parts we're talking about.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: A fraction has two parts — the numerator (top) tells you how many pieces you want, and the denominator (bottom) tells you how many equal pieces the whole is divided into. 1/2 means 1 out of 2 equal pieces.
rounds.goal: Learn what fractions mean by slicing your first pizza correctly.
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon pizza shop kitchen on opening day, young chef holding pizza cutter over a whole pizza, Chef Maria pointing at the pizza, warm welcoming atmosphere, Pixar-style
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is it important that both halves of a pizza are exactly equal in size?
rounds.scene_hint: Cartoon pizza shop kitchen on opening day, young chef holding pizza cutter over a whole pizza, Chef Maria pointing at the pizza, warm welcoming atmosphere, Pixar-style
rounds.situation: It is your first day running the Fraction Pizza Shop! Chef Maria shows you around the kitchen. Your first customer walks in and asks for 'half a pepperoni pizza.' Sounds simple, right? But do you know what 1/2 really means when you are holding a pizza cutter?
rounds.title: Day 1: Welcome to the Kitchen

choices.label: A. 2/4, 3/6, and 4/8 are all equivalent to 1/2
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Equivalent fractions represent the same amount. If you multiply BOTH the numerator and denominator by the same number, you get an equivalent fraction: 1/2 = (1×2)/(2×2) = 2/4 = (1×3)/(2×3) = 3/6 = (1×4)/(2×4) = 4/8. They all equal one half!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.creativity: Thinking outside the box leads to more original solutions.

choices.label: B. 2/4 is equivalent to 1/2 but 3/6 is NOT
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Both 2/4 AND 3/6 are equivalent to 1/2. Check: 3/6 — divide both numerator and denominator by 3: 3÷3 = 1, 6÷3 = 2, giving us 1/2. The rule works for ANY number you multiply or divide both parts by!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. 1/2 = 2/3 because you add 1 to both top and bottom
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You CANNOT make equivalent fractions by ADDING the same number to top and bottom. 1/2 ≠ 2/3. To find equivalent fractions, you must MULTIPLY (or divide) both numerator and denominator by the same number. 1/2 = (1×2)/(2×2) = 2/4 ✓

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/5 because the top goes up by 1 each time
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 3/5 is NOT equivalent to 1/2. For equivalent fractions, multiply BOTH parts by the SAME number. 1/2 → multiply by 2 → 2/4 ✓. 1/2 → multiply by 3 → 3/6 ✓ (not 3/5). The denominator must change by the same factor as the numerator.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Consistency matters in fractions. 1/2 always means exactly one out of two equal parts — not 'sort of half' or 'close to half.' Precision builds trust.
rounds.goal: Practice making perfect halves consistently across multiple pizzas.
rounds.image_prompt: Three cartoon pizzas on a counter, each split perfectly in half with different colorful toppings on each side, chef proudly presenting them, warm kitchen background
rounds.reflection_prompt: If one half of a pizza is bigger than the other, is it really divided into halves? Why or why not?
rounds.scene_hint: Three cartoon pizzas on a counter, each split perfectly in half with different colorful toppings on each side, chef proudly presenting them, warm kitchen background
rounds.situation: Your shop's signature pizza is the 'Half-and-Half Special' — one half with one topping, the other half with a different topping. Today three families order it, but each wants different topping combinations. You need to make sure each half is truly 1/2 of the pizza.
rounds.title: Day 2: The Half-and-Half Special

choices.label: A. 3/4 is larger than 2/3 because 9/12 > 8/12
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To compare fractions with different denominators, find a common denominator. LCD of 4 and 3 is 12. Convert: 3/4 = 9/12 and 2/3 = 8/12. Since 9/12 > 8/12, we know 3/4 > 2/3. Always convert to the same denominator before comparing!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. 2/3 is larger than 3/4 because 3 is a smaller denominator
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A smaller denominator does NOT automatically make a fraction larger. To compare properly, find the LCD (12): 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Since 9/12 > 8/12, 3/4 is actually the larger fraction. Always convert to a common denominator!

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: C. They are equal because 3+4 = 2+3+2
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You cannot compare fractions by adding their parts. 3/4 ≠ 2/3. The correct method: find LCD of 4 and 3, which is 12. Then 3/4 = 9/12 and 2/3 = 8/12. Since 9 > 8, we see 3/4 > 2/3.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: D. 2/3 is larger because 2×4 = 8 and 3×3 = 9 wait... they're equal
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Cross-multiplication CAN help compare: 3×3 = 9 (left) vs 2×4 = 8 (right). Since 9 > 8, the LEFT fraction (3/4) is larger. They're NOT equal. You had the right idea with cross-multiplication but made an error in the comparison!

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: To make quarters, cut the pizza in half, then cut each half in half again. 1/4 means 1 out of 4 equal pieces. 3/4 means 3 out of 4 equal pieces.
rounds.goal: Master cutting pizzas into quarters (1/4) and understand what 3/4 means.
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon pizza cut into four perfect equal quarters, each quarter with a different colored plate underneath, four happy friends reaching for their slices, bright kitchen
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you eat 1/4 of a pizza and your friend eats 2/4, who ate more? How do you know?
rounds.scene_hint: Cartoon pizza cut into four perfect equal quarters, each quarter with a different colored plate underneath, four happy friends reaching for their slices, bright kitchen
rounds.situation: A group of four friends walks in and wants to share one large pizza equally. Each person should get exactly 1/4 of the pizza. Meanwhile, another customer wants 3/4 of a pizza to take home. You need to cut pizzas into quarters today!
rounds.title: Day 3: Quarter Portions

choices.label: A. 12/18 simplified = 2/3 (divide both by GCF of 6)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To simplify 12/18, find the Greatest Common Factor (GCF) of 12 and 18. Factors of 12: 1,2,3,4,6,12. Factors of 18: 1,2,3,6,9,18. GCF = 6. Divide both by 6: 12÷6 = 2, 18÷6 = 3. So 12/18 = 2/3. A fraction is fully simplified when the only common factor is 1.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. 12/18 simplified = 6/9 (divide both by 2)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 While 6/9 IS equivalent to 12/18, it's not fully simplified! 6 and 9 still share a common factor of 3. Divide again: 6÷3 = 2, 9÷3 = 3 → 2/3. To simplify completely in one step, use the GCF (6): 12÷6 = 2, 18÷6 = 3.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. 12/18 simplified = 1/6 (subtract 12-11 and 18-12)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Simplifying fractions means DIVIDING both numerator and denominator by the same number — never subtracting! To simplify 12/18: find GCF of 12 and 18 (it's 6), then divide both: 12÷6 = 2, 18÷6 = 3. Answer: 2/3.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. 12/18 simplified = 4/6 (divide both by 3)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 4/6 is equivalent to 12/18, but NOT fully simplified. 4 and 6 still share a common factor of 2! Divide again: 4÷2 = 2, 6÷2 = 3 → 2/3. Tip: Use the GCF to simplify in one step — GCF(12,18) = 6, so 12÷6 / 18÷6 = 2/3.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Thirds are harder than halves because you cannot just fold or cross-cut. You need to think about angles — each third is 120 degrees of the circle. 1/3 means 1 out of 3 equal pieces.
rounds.goal: Learn to divide pizzas into thirds (1/3) and understand this trickier fraction.
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon pizza being carefully divided into three equal sections with three different colorful toppings, protractor visible, Chef Maria guiding young chef, geometric lines drawn on pizza
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is cutting something into 3 equal pieces harder than cutting it into 2 or 4 equal pieces?
rounds.scene_hint: Cartoon pizza being carefully divided into three equal sections with three different colorful toppings, protractor visible, Chef Maria guiding young chef, geometric lines drawn on pizza
rounds.situation: Chef Maria introduces a new 'Thirds Menu' — pizzas divided into three equal parts, each with a different premium topping. But cutting a circle into three equal pieces is much harder than halves or quarters! Marco is struggling and looking to you for help.
rounds.title: Day 4: Third of the Menu

widget_answer.prompt: What fraction of the pizza has been eaten?

choices.label: A. 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7 (add numerators, keep denominator)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When fractions have the SAME denominator, simply add the numerators and keep the denominator the same. 2/7 + 3/7 = (2+3)/7 = 5/7. Think of it like adding apples: 2 sevenths + 3 sevenths = 5 sevenths!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/14 (add tops and add bottoms)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 When adding fractions, you do NOT add the denominators! The denominator tells us the SIZE of each piece — it stays the same. 2/7 + 3/7 = (2+3)/7 = 5/7. Think: 2 slices + 3 slices = 5 slices (the slices are still sevenths).

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: C. 2/7 + 3/7 = 6/7 (multiply 2×3 = 6)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 We need to ADD the numerators, not multiply them. 2+3 = 5, not 2×3 = 6. The correct answer is 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7. Remember: addition means combining, not multiplying!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: D. 2/7 + 3/7 = 1 (because 2+3 = 5 and 5/7 rounds to 1)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 While 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7 is close to 1, it is NOT equal to 1. To make 1, you'd need 7/7. So 5/7 is 2/7 less than a whole. Always give exact fraction answers — don't round unless asked!

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: A mixed number like 2 1/2 means 2 whole pizzas plus 1/2 of another pizza. You can also write this as 5/2 (an improper fraction). Both represent the same amount!
rounds.goal: Understand mixed numbers and improper fractions in real pizza orders.
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon soccer team celebrating in pizza shop, two whole pizzas and one half-pizza on the table, kids in jerseys cheering, festive atmosphere, party decorations
rounds.reflection_prompt: If someone orders 1 and 1/2 pizzas, is that the same as ordering 3/2 of a pizza? How can you check?
rounds.scene_hint: Cartoon soccer team celebrating in pizza shop, two whole pizzas and one half-pizza on the table, kids in jerseys cheering, festive atmosphere, party decorations
rounds.situation: A soccer team just won their match and comes to celebrate! Their coach orders '2 and 1/2 pizzas' for the team. Then a family orders '1 and 3/4 pizzas' for dinner. These are mixed numbers — a whole number combined with a fraction. How do you handle orders bigger than one pizza?
rounds.title: Day 5: Mixed Number Madness

challenge.question: What is 1/3 + 1/6? Express as a decimal (round to 2 places).

choices.label: A. 1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12 (LCD is 12: 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To add fractions with different denominators, find the Least Common Denominator (LCD). LCD of 3 and 4 is 12. Convert: 1/3 = 4/12 (multiply top and bottom by 4) and 1/4 = 3/12 (multiply top and bottom by 3). Now add: 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Resisting the quick fix in favor of lasting results shows maturity.

choices.label: B. 1/3 + 1/4 = 2/7 (add tops and bottoms separately)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 This is the most common fraction mistake! You CANNOT add fractions by adding numerators and denominators separately. 1/3 + 1/4 ≠ 2/7. You need a common denominator first. LCD of 3 and 4 = 12. So: 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. 1/3 + 1/4 = 2/12 (multiply denominators, add numerators)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You found the right common denominator (12) but forgot to convert the numerators! When changing 1/3 to twelfths: 1/3 = 4/12 (not 1/12). When changing 1/4 to twelfths: 1/4 = 3/12 (not 1/12). So 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. 1/3 + 1/4 = 1/7 (add the denominators for the new bottom)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The common denominator is NOT found by adding denominators (3+4=7). The LCD of 3 and 4 is 12 (smallest number both divide into). Convert: 1/3 = 4/12, 1/4 = 3/12. Then add: 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: To add 1/4 + 1/2, you need a common denominator. Since 1/2 = 2/4, the problem becomes 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4. Always convert fractions to the same denominator before adding!
rounds.goal: Learn to add fractions with different denominators by finding common denominators.
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon kitchen scene with measuring cups showing 1/4 and 1/2, a recipe card on the wall, pizza dough being prepared with sauce ingredients, mathematical equations floating in the air, fun educational style
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why can you not just add 1/4 + 1/2 and get 2/6? What is wrong with adding numerators and denominators separately?
rounds.scene_hint: Cartoon kitchen scene with measuring cups showing 1/4 and 1/2, a recipe card on the wall, pizza dough being prepared with sauce ingredients, mathematical equations floating in the air, fun educational style
rounds.situation: Chef Maria reveals her secret recipe for the ultimate pizza sauce. The recipe calls for 1/4 cup of tomato paste plus 1/2 cup of crushed tomatoes. But wait — what is 1/4 + 1/2? You need to add fractions to follow the recipe! And a customer wants 1/4 of a pizza with extra cheese and 1/2 with olives — that means 3/4 is covered. What fraction has no topping?
rounds.title: Day 6: The Fraction Recipe

choices.label: A. 5/6 − 1/4 = 7/12 (LCD is 12: 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Subtracting fractions works just like adding — find the LCD first! LCD of 6 and 4 is 12. Convert: 5/6 = 10/12 (×2) and 1/4 = 3/12 (×3). Subtract the numerators: 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12. The denominator stays the same!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: B. 5/6 − 1/4 = 4/2 (subtract tops and bottoms: 5−1=4, 6−4=2)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You cannot subtract numerators and denominators separately! First find the LCD of 6 and 4, which is 12. Convert: 5/6 = 10/12 and 1/4 = 3/12. Then subtract numerators only: 10 − 3 = 7. Answer: 7/12.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. 5/6 − 1/4 = 10/12 (I converted 5/6 but forgot to subtract)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You correctly converted 5/6 to 10/12, but you need to actually subtract! 1/4 = 3/12. Now subtract: 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12. Converting is just the first step — don't forget to finish the operation!

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. 5/6 − 1/4 = 4/6 (just subtract the numerators: 5−1=4)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You can only subtract numerators directly when the denominators are the SAME. 5/6 and 1/4 have different denominators. First convert to LCD 12: 5/6 = 10/12, 1/4 = 3/12. Then 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Real-world math happens under pressure. When you truly understand fractions — not just memorize — you can perform even when stressed. Deep knowledge beats surface memorization.
rounds.goal: Apply all your fraction skills under pressure — speed AND accuracy matter now!
rounds.image_prompt: Chaotic cartoon pizza kitchen during lunch rush, orders piling up on counter, multiple pizzas being cut simultaneously, stressed but determined young chef, clock on wall showing noon, steam and energy everywhere
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does understanding fractions deeply (not just memorizing) help you perform under pressure?
rounds.scene_hint: Chaotic cartoon pizza kitchen during lunch rush, orders piling up on counter, multiple pizzas being cut simultaneously, stressed but determined young chef, clock on wall showing noon, steam and energy everywhere
rounds.situation: CRISIS! The entire school across the street just let out early and 40 hungry students flood your shop at once! Orders are flying in: '1/2 pepperoni!' '3/4 veggie!' '2/3 cheese!' '1/4 mushroom!' You need to calculate fractions fast under extreme pressure. Marco looks panicked. Chef Maria is shouting orders. The kitchen is chaos!
rounds.title: Day 7: Lunch Rush Disaster!

widget_answer.prompt: Express the sale discount as a fraction

choices.label: A. 2 3/4 = 11/4 (because 2×4 + 3 = 11, over 4)
choices.learning_concept: Converting Mixed Numbers to Improper Fractions
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To convert a mixed number to an improper fraction: multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator. 2 3/4: 2 × 4 = 8, then 8 + 3 = 11. Keep the same denominator: 11/4. This means 2 whole pizzas (8/4) plus 3/4 = 11/4.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. 2 3/4 = 23/4 (just put the 2 and 3 together as 23)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You can't just stick the numbers together! The correct method: multiply whole number × denominator, then add the numerator. 2 3/4: 2×4=8, then 8+3=11. Answer: 11/4. Think of it as: 2 wholes = 8 quarters, plus 3 more quarters = 11 quarters.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. 2 3/4 = 5/4 (just add 2+3 = 5 over 4)
choices.learning_concept: Mixed Number Conversion — Multiply Then Add
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You added the whole number and numerator (2+3=5), but you need to MULTIPLY the whole number by the denominator first, THEN add. 2×4=8, then 8+3=11. So 2 3/4 = 11/4. Note: 5/4 = 1 1/4, which is much less than 2 3/4!

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. 2 3/4 = 6/4 (multiply 2×3 = 6 over 4)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You multiplied the whole number by the numerator (2×3=6) instead of by the denominator. Correct method: multiply whole × denominator: 2×4=8, then ADD the numerator: 8+3=11. Answer: 11/4. Remember: whole × denominator + numerator!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: To multiply a fraction by a whole number, multiply the numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator. 24 x 1/3 = 24/3 = 8 pizzas. Or think of it as: if 3 kids share one pizza, then 24 / 3 = 8 pizzas needed.
rounds.goal: Learn to multiply a fraction by a whole number to calculate bulk orders.
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon school teacher at pizza shop counter with clipboard, young chef calculating on paper, stacks of pizza boxes being prepared, number 24 and fraction 1/3 floating as thought bubbles
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does 24 x 1/3 give the same answer as 24 / 3? What does this tell us about fractions and division?
rounds.scene_hint: Cartoon school teacher at pizza shop counter with clipboard, young chef calculating on paper, stacks of pizza boxes being prepared, number 24 and fraction 1/3 floating as thought bubbles
rounds.situation: A school teacher orders pizzas for a class of 24 students. She says: 'Each child should get exactly 1/3 of a pizza.' You need to figure out how many whole pizzas to make. That means multiplying a fraction by a whole number: 24 times 1/3. Can you do it?
rounds.title: Day 8: Pizza Party Planning

choices.label: A. 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15 (multiply tops: 2×4=8, bottoms: 3×5=15)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Multiplying fractions is straightforward: multiply the numerators together and multiply the denominators together. 2/3 × 4/5 = (2×4)/(3×5) = 8/15. No need for common denominators when multiplying — just straight across!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. 2/3 × 4/5 = 6/8 (add tops: 2+4=6, add bottoms: 3+5=8)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You added instead of multiplying! For multiplication, multiply across: numerator × numerator and denominator × denominator. 2/3 × 4/5 = (2×4)/(3×5) = 8/15. Adding tops and bottoms is not correct for any fraction operation!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/5 (multiply tops: 2×4=8, keep larger bottom: 5)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You correctly multiplied the numerators (2×4=8) but forgot to multiply the denominators. Both parts get multiplied: 3×5=15, not just keeping 5. The answer is 8/15. When multiplying fractions, multiply BOTH top and bottom.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/3 (multiply tops: 2×4=8, keep first bottom: 3)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You multiplied the numerators correctly (2×4=8) but kept only the first denominator. In fraction multiplication, both denominators multiply too: 3×5=15. So 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15. Remember: multiply straight across, top AND bottom!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: To compare 2/3 and 3/4, find a common denominator (12). Convert: 2/3 = 8/12, 3/4 = 9/12. Since 9/12 > 8/12, we know 3/4 > 2/3. The customer with 3/4 gets more pizza!
rounds.goal: Learn to compare fractions by finding common denominators or using cross-multiplication.
rounds.image_prompt: Two cartoon customers at a pizza counter, one holding 2/3 pizza and the other holding 3/4 pizza, comparison symbols between them, young chef as judge with thinking pose, balance scale in background
rounds.reflection_prompt: Just because a fraction has a bigger numerator, does that mean it is a bigger fraction? Why or why not?
rounds.scene_hint: Two cartoon customers at a pizza counter, one holding 2/3 pizza and the other holding 3/4 pizza, comparison symbols between them, young chef as judge with thinking pose, balance scale in background
rounds.situation: Two customers are arguing at the counter! Customer A says she ordered 2/3 of a pizza and Customer B says he ordered 3/4 of a pizza. They both claim they should get the bigger portion. You need to figure out: which fraction is larger, 2/3 or 3/4? The whole shop is watching to see if you can settle this!
rounds.title: Day 9: Comparing Customer Orders

challenge.question: A pizza has 8 slices. You eat 3/8 and your friend eats 2/8. What fraction is left? (as decimal)

choices.label: A. 3/4 ÷ 2/5 = 15/8 (flip second fraction: 3/4 × 5/2 = 15/8)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To divide fractions, use Keep-Change-Flip (KCF): KEEP the first fraction (3/4), CHANGE ÷ to ×, FLIP the second fraction (2/5 becomes 5/2). Then multiply: 3/4 × 5/2 = 15/8 = 1 7/8. Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.creativity: Exploring an unconventional approach shows creative thinking.

choices.label: B. 3/4 ÷ 2/5 = 6/20 (multiply straight across: 3×2=6, 4×5=20)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 That's the rule for multiplication, not division! For division, you must FLIP the second fraction first. 3/4 ÷ 2/5 = 3/4 × 5/2 = 15/8. Remember KCF: Keep the first, Change ÷ to ×, Flip the second.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. 3/4 ÷ 2/5 = 4/3 × 2/5 = 8/15 (flip the FIRST fraction)
choices.learning_concept: Flip the Second Fraction Not the First
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You flipped the wrong fraction! In Keep-Change-Flip, you KEEP the first fraction (3/4) and FLIP the second (2/5 → 5/2). So: 3/4 × 5/2 = 15/8. Always flip the divisor (the fraction after the ÷ sign).

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. 3/4 ÷ 2/5 = 1/9 (divide tops: 3÷2≈1, divide bottoms: 4÷5≈1... not sure)
choices.learning_concept: Cannot Divide Numerators and Denominators Separately
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Dividing tops and bottoms separately doesn't work for fraction division. Use KCF: Keep 3/4, Change ÷ to ×, Flip 2/5 to 5/2. Then multiply: 3×5=15, 4×2=8. Answer: 15/8 or 1 7/8.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Equivalent fractions look different but represent the same amount. 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8 = 5/10. To check, simplify by dividing numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor.
rounds.goal: Master equivalent fractions — different numbers that represent the same amount.
rounds.image_prompt: Three identical cartoon pizzas cut differently — one in 8 slices with 4 shaded, one in 4 slices with 2 shaded, one in 6 slices with 3 shaded — all showing the same half portion, colorful comparison display
rounds.reflection_prompt: Can you think of three different fractions that are all equal to 1/3? How did you find them?
rounds.scene_hint: Three identical cartoon pizzas cut differently — one in 8 slices with 4 shaded, one in 4 slices with 2 shaded, one in 6 slices with 3 shaded — all showing the same half portion, colorful comparison display
rounds.situation: Chef Maria declares it 'Equivalent Fraction Day' — a promotion where customers can order their pizza sliced any way they want as long as they get the same total amount. One customer wants 4/8 of a pizza. Another wants 2/4. A third wants 3/6. Are these all the same amount? You need to prove it!
rounds.title: Day 10: Equivalent Fraction Day

choices.label: A. 3/4 of 32 = 24 (divide 32 by 4 = 8, then multiply 8 × 3 = 24)
choices.learning_concept: Finding a Fraction of a Whole Number
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To find a fraction of a number, divide by the denominator first, then multiply by the numerator. 3/4 of 32: Step 1: 32 ÷ 4 = 8 (that gives us one quarter). Step 2: 8 × 3 = 24 (three quarters). So 3/4 of 32 = 24!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. 3/4 of 32 = 12 (32 ÷ 4 = 8, then 8 + 4 = 12)
choices.learning_concept: Fractions of Amounts — Multiply Not Add
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You found 1/4 of 32 correctly (32÷4=8) but then added 4 instead of multiplying by 3. For 3/4 of 32: first find 1/4 (32÷4=8), then multiply by 3 (8×3=24). The numerator tells you how many parts to take!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. 3/4 of 32 = 96 (32 × 3 = 96, ignore the 4)
choices.learning_concept: Fractions of Amounts — Must Divide by Denominator
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A fraction of a number is always SMALLER than (or equal to) the number itself! 3/4 of 32 can't be 96. You need to divide by the denominator too: 32 ÷ 4 = 8, then 8 × 3 = 24. Or think: 32 × 3/4 = 96/4 = 24.

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: D. 3/4 of 32 = 8 (just divide 32 by 4)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 32 ÷ 4 = 8 gives you 1/4 of 32, not 3/4. You found one quarter but forgot to multiply by the numerator (3). Three-quarters means 3 groups of one-quarter: 8 × 3 = 24. So 3/4 of 32 = 24.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Subtracting fractions with the same denominator is simple — just subtract the numerators! 3/4 - 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2. Priya ate exactly half the pizza. For unlike denominators, find a common denominator first.
rounds.goal: Learn to subtract fractions and apply it to real kitchen problems.
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon pizza with one quarter missing, fraction equation 3/4 - 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2 shown above, Picky Priya character pointing at leftover slice, calculator and receipt visible, pizza shop counter
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you have 7/8 of a pizza and eat 3/8, what fraction is left? What if the denominators were different?
rounds.scene_hint: Cartoon pizza with one quarter missing, fraction equation 3/4 - 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2 shown above, Picky Priya character pointing at leftover slice, calculator and receipt visible, pizza shop counter
rounds.situation: Picky Priya orders 3/4 of a pizza, eats some, and then returns with 1/4 left over asking for a refund on the uneaten portion. You need to calculate: 3/4 - 1/4 = ? to figure out how much she ate. Meanwhile, a catering order needs you to figure out: you have 5/6 of your dough supply left and a recipe uses 2/6. How much dough remains after baking?
rounds.title: Day 11: Subtraction Station

choices.label: A. She has 5/12 of the cake left (started with 3/4 = 9/12, ate 1/3 = 4/12, so 9/12 − 4/12 = 5/12)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Word problem strategy: Riya has 3/4 of a cake and eats 1/3 of the whole cake. LCD of 4 and 3 is 12. Convert: 3/4 = 9/12, 1/3 = 4/12. Subtract: 9/12 − 4/12 = 5/12. She has 5/12 of the cake left. Always convert to common denominators in word problems too!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Waiting for the right moment instead of rushing shows self-control.

choices.label: B. She has 2/1 left (3−1=2 and 4−3=1, so 2/1)
choices.learning_concept: Word Problems — Cannot Subtract Parts Separately
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You cannot subtract numerators and denominators separately! To find 3/4 − 1/3, find the LCD (12). Convert: 3/4 = 9/12, 1/3 = 4/12. Subtract: 9/12 − 4/12 = 5/12. In word problems, always set up the fraction equation first.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: C. She has 2/12 left (3/4 − 1/3 = 3/12 − 1/12 = 2/12)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You found the right LCD (12) but converted incorrectly. 3/4 = 9/12 (multiply both by 3), not 3/12. And 1/3 = 4/12 (multiply both by 4), not 1/12. So: 9/12 − 4/12 = 5/12. Remember to multiply BOTH parts of each fraction.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: D. She has 7/12 left (3/4 + 1/3 = 9/12 + 4/12 = 13/12... wait, I should subtract not add)
choices.learning_concept: Word Problems — Choosing the Right Operation
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You correctly identified you should subtract (not add), and your conversions are right (3/4 = 9/12, 1/3 = 4/12). The answer is 9/12 − 4/12 = 5/12, not 7/12. Read word problems carefully: 'eats' = subtract, 'gets more' = add.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Complex fraction problems are just simple steps chained together. Convert 1/4 to 2/8. Then: 5/8 + 2/8 = 7/8 covered. So 1 - 7/8 = 1/8 is plain cheese. Break big problems into small steps!
rounds.goal: Combine addition, subtraction, and equivalent fractions to solve a complex multi-step fraction problem under pressure.
rounds.image_prompt: Intimidating cartoon food critic with notepad sitting at a table, sweating young chef carefully preparing a pizza with precisely measured fraction sections, dramatic spotlight on the pizza, tension in the air
rounds.reflection_prompt: When you face a math problem with multiple steps, how does breaking it into smaller parts make it less scary?
rounds.scene_hint: Intimidating cartoon food critic with notepad sitting at a table, sweating young chef carefully preparing a pizza with precisely measured fraction sections, dramatic spotlight on the pizza, tension in the air
rounds.situation: CRISIS! The city's most famous food critic, known for being brutally honest, walks into your shop. She orders a very specific pizza: '5/8 pepperoni, 1/4 mushroom, and the rest plain cheese.' You need to figure out the exact fractions — what fraction is plain cheese? That requires: 1 - 5/8 - 1/4 = ? If you get this wrong, the review will destroy your reputation!
rounds.title: Day 12: The Food Critic!

challenge.question: If 3/4 of a class of 32 students passed, how many passed?

choices.label: A. 5/8 is between 1/2 and 3/4 on the number line (because 4/8 < 5/8 < 6/8)
choices.learning_concept: Placing Fractions on a Number Line
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To place 5/8 on a number line, convert nearby fractions to eighths: 1/2 = 4/8 and 3/4 = 6/8. Since 4/8 < 5/8 < 6/8, the fraction 5/8 sits between 1/2 and 3/4. Using a common denominator makes it easy to see the order!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.creativity: Looking at the problem from a new angle demonstrates creativity.

choices.label: B. 5/8 is between 0 and 1/4 because 5 and 8 are small numbers
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 5/8 means 5 out of 8 equal parts, which is more than half! 1/4 = 2/8, and 5/8 is much larger than 2/8. On the number line, 5/8 sits between 1/2 (=4/8) and 3/4 (=6/8). Think of it as being just past the halfway mark.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. 5/8 is exactly at 3/4 because they're close enough
choices.learning_concept: Fractions Are Exact Points on Number Line
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Close is not the same as equal! 5/8 ≠ 3/4. Convert to the same denominator: 5/8 stays as 5/8, and 3/4 = 6/8. Since 5 ≠ 6, they're different fractions. 5/8 is 1/8 less than 3/4. Every fraction has its own exact spot on the number line.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. 5/8 is between 3/4 and 1 because the numerator (5) is bigger than half of 8
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 While 5 IS more than half of 8, that puts 5/8 above 1/2, not above 3/4. Convert: 3/4 = 6/8. Since 5/8 < 6/8, we see 5/8 is actually BELOW 3/4. So 5/8 sits between 1/2 (4/8) and 3/4 (6/8).

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Fractions are not just numbers — they describe parts of a whole. When you can visualize fractions as colors, shapes, and patterns, you truly understand them. 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/8 = 1 whole!
rounds.goal: Use fractions creatively to design visually stunning pizzas — fraction art!
rounds.image_prompt: Beautiful artistic cartoon pizza designed as fraction art, different colorful sections showing 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 with vibrant toppings, art gallery setting, easel next to pizza, creative and educational, Pixar-style
rounds.reflection_prompt: How does seeing fractions as parts of a real thing (like a pizza) help you understand them better than just seeing numbers on paper?
rounds.scene_hint: Beautiful artistic cartoon pizza designed as fraction art, different colorful sections showing 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 with vibrant toppings, art gallery setting, easel next to pizza, creative and educational, Pixar-style
rounds.situation: A local art school wants you to create 'Fraction Art Pizzas' for their exhibition opening! Each pizza should be a visual representation of fractions using different colored toppings. The challenge: create a pizza that shows 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, and 1/8 as four distinct sections. Can you make math look beautiful and delicious?
rounds.title: Day 13: Creative Pizza Design

choices.label: A. 3/8 = 0.375 (divide 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator. 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. You can check: 0.375 × 8 = 3 ✓. Some common ones to remember: 1/2 = 0.5, 1/4 = 0.25, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/8 = 0.125.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.
skill_explanation.creativity: Combining ideas in unexpected ways shows innovative thinking.

choices.label: B. 3/8 = 0.38 (just write the numbers as a decimal: 3-8 → 0.38)
choices.learning_concept: Fraction to Decimal — Division Not Concatenation
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You can't just place the digits next to each other! To convert a fraction to a decimal, you must DIVIDE: 3 ÷ 8. Do the long division: 3.000 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Check: 0.38 × 8 = 3.04 (not 3!), but 0.375 × 8 = 3 ✓.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. 3/8 = 2.67 (divide 8 ÷ 3 = 2.666... ≈ 2.67)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You divided the wrong way around! For 3/8, divide the numerator BY the denominator: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 (not 8 ÷ 3 = 2.67). A proper fraction (numerator < denominator) always converts to a decimal less than 1.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. 3/8 = 0.3 (because the numerator is 3, so just put 0.3)
choices.learning_concept: Fraction to Decimal Requires Full Division
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The numerator alone doesn't give you the decimal. You need to do the full division: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. While 3/10 = 0.3 (because dividing by 10 is easy), 3/8 is different since we're dividing by 8, not 10.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Everything you have learned builds on itself. Halves led to quarters, quarters led to eighths, understanding equivalence let you compare and convert, and operations let you solve real problems. Fractions are a complete toolkit!
rounds.goal: Showcase all your fraction knowledge by creating the ultimate demonstration pizza and running the event smoothly.
rounds.image_prompt: Grand opening celebration at cartoon pizza shop, red ribbon being cut, mayor and newspaper reporter, showcase pizza on a pedestal with fraction labels, balloons, confetti, proud young chef and full kitchen crew, festive Pixar-style
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back over the past 14 days, which fraction concept was hardest for you? Which are you most proud of mastering?

rounds.situation: It is the Grand Opening of your newly rebranded 'Fraction Pizza Shop!' The mayor is coming to cut the ribbon (and a pizza). The local newspaper is covering the event. You need to prepare a showcase pizza that demonstrates everything you have learned: halves, thirds, quarters, addition, subtraction, equivalent fractions, and mixed numbers. This is your moment to shine!
